scenes.text: Two floors of an office look exactly alike. Why does a good SLAM system fold them into one?
scenes.say: Two floors of an office look exactly alike. Why does a perfectly good mapping system fold them into one?

scenes.headline: How a SLAM system keeps identical floors apart
scenes.sub: And how GNSS and calibration tools refuse wrong answers
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Ondine! Today, an open system that keeps a building's floors apart, and two more tools with the same habit: refusing an answer they cannot support.

scenes.title: Why identical floors merge
scenes.sub: A precise constraint that is completely wrong
scenes.say: Chapter one. Why identical floors merge.

scenes.title: How a loop closure is made

steps.say: A robot walks the corridor on floor one. Three metres below, floor zero has the same corridor, scanned earlier.

steps.term: Place recognizer: finds where you have been
steps.say: The place recognizer compares descriptors and says, correctly, these two places look the same.
Registration checks the match. The walls really do line up, to a few centimetres.

steps.term: Loop factor: a precise relative pose
steps.say: So the graph gets a loop factor: precise, consistent, and wrong. It says two places three metres apart are one.

labels: One false loop: floor 1 at 0.30 m
35 false loops: one floor, not two

steps.say: Make it one number: floor one's height. The stairs say three metres, give or take fifteen centimetres.
One false loop says zero, give or take five centimetres. It outvotes the stairs nine to one, and floor one drops to thirty centimetres.
Add the rest of the false loops, and floor one lands on floor zero. A barometer would only slow the slide.
Switch the gate on, and the loops are never written. Floor one goes back to three metres, however many matches there were.
The project tests this on purpose. Two identical floors, joined by stairs, camera only.
With the floor gate switched off by a debug flag, the recognizer proposes thirty five matches across floors.
All of them are accepted, along with six real ones.

steps.term: Collapse rate: loops joining different floors
steps.say: Thirty five of forty one loops join different floors. The map ends with one floor instead of two, and the test passes only because it collapsed.

scenes.title: A graph per floor
scenes.sub: Make the wrong factor impossible to write
scenes.say: Chapter two. A graph per floor.

scenes.text: Keep a separate map for every floor, and refuse every loop closure between floors. Join the floors later, offline.
scenes.mark: refuse every loop closure between floors
scenes.say: The idea is blunt. Keep a separate map for every floor, refuse every loop closure between floors, and join the floors later, offline.

steps.say: First, something says the robot left its floor: tracked height, the barometer, or the accelerometer feeling an elevator push.
The floor manager waits until everything is calm again.

steps.term: Elevator: pressure climbs, the camera sees none
steps.say: Then it classifies. If the pressure climbed but the camera saw no climb, it was an elevator. Otherwise stairs or a ramp, split by slope.
Finally the climb is snapped to a whole number of storeys, so a half landing on the stairs never becomes a floor.
Every candidate loop passes through a gate before it reaches a graph. Open it, and there are three separate checks.
First, each floor has its own place database, so a scan is only ever compared with its own floor.
Second, a loop whose two ends carry different floor labels is rejected.
Third, each floor's graph refuses a factor to a node it does not hold. No code path can join two floors.
Their demo shows it in simulation. Without the gate, loop closures pile the two floors together.
With it, each floor stays in its own map, and the stairs join them.

And on real data, a hand-held LiDAR rides an elevator. The accelerometer measures the ride the LiDAR cannot see, the new floor gets its own colour, and the walk back down the stairs is measured by the odometry.

scenes.title: The same habit elsewhere
scenes.say: Chapter three. The same habit elsewhere.

steps.say: Satellite code ranges give a position to a few metres.

steps.term: Double difference: rover minus base, minus reference
steps.say: Differencing against a base station and a reference satellite cancels both clocks.
What remains is a whole number of carrier cycles per satellite, which the filter estimates as real numbers.
An integer least squares search finds the best set and the runner up.
The library fixes only if the runner up is three times worse. Otherwise it stays float, rather than report false confidence.
A calibration checker does the same. Here a LiDAR transform carries an injected yaw error, and the points miss the bollards.
It judges the error against the data's own noise and fails the pair. An axis the recording could not observe is marked not measured, never guessed.

scenes.title: What is not proven yet
scenes.say: The floor gate is sound by construction. The rest has thinner evidence.

items.text: The simulated camera sees features, not images
items.say: The simulator's camera produces feature points, not rendered images, so the visual front end's real failures are not in those tests.
Real multi-floor evidence is one elevator dataset and a few robot bags.

items.text: Wall matching never helped on real data
items.say: And matching walls between floors has not yet contributed a constraint on real data.

scenes.text: The safest estimator is one that cannot write the wrong answer down.
scenes.mark: cannot write the wrong answer down
scenes.say: The common thread: the safest estimator is one that cannot write the wrong answer down.

recap: One map per floor, no loops between
Integers fixed only past a ratio test
scenes.say: To recap. One map per floor, with no loops between. Integers fixed only past a ratio test. And calibration checked, axis by axis.
